who.lede: Scanning to e-mail is already built into almost every office machine. The only thing stopping it is that somebody has to find a mail server, a port, a user name and a password first. Pick the situation that sounds like yours.
who.p1.a: At home, scanning is set up for one person — the one who set up the router in the first place. Everyone else carries their documents to them and waits. Or photographs them with a phone and sends a blurry image.
who.p1.b: The printer is set up once. After that, everyone types their own address on the device screen and the scan goes straight to them — nothing has to be registered in advance.
who.p1.o: The last time anyone at home has to ask for help with scanning.
who.p2.h: The IT queue that never ends
who.p2.a: SMTP has to be set up again for every printer, every new employee and every brand. Canon, HP, Brother, Kyocera — a different menu, different names. There is no single set of instructions that fits the whole fleet.
who.p2.b: Each device becomes a separate line in the account, with its own credentials. One process for the whole fleet, and the machine in the corridor can be switched off without touching the rest.
who.p2.o: A new employee gets an address, not a trip to the printer.
who.p3.a: Since January 2020, SMTP AUTH has been off by default for new Microsoft 365 tenants, and at the end of December 2026 Microsoft will turn it off by default for existing ones too. A printer that sent scans for years simply stops one morning.
who.p3.b: The device sends through our SMTP, not through your 365 tenant. You do not need a static IP address, an open port 25, an Azure subscription, or OAuth support on a machine that will never get it.
who.p3.o: Scans reach outside recipients again — a client, an accountant, the bank.
who.p4.h: You have bought a new machine
who.p4.a: The printer has been replaced, and every setting left with the old one. Nobody remembers the exact values, so scanning is down until someone finds the time to set it up again.
who.p4.b: Add the new device to the account and get new credentials for it. The address the scans arrive at stays the same — only the hardware under it changes.
who.p4.o: Nothing has to be remembered from last time and nothing has to be carried over by hand.
how.h2: From buying a printer to a working digital habit
how.lede: Most people meet this problem the same way: they buy or inherit a printer, notice it already claims to do Scan-to-Email, and then get stuck on the SMTP screen. ScanInbox skips straight from “I have a printer” to “it emails me the scan” — one guided setup, then it just works, for as long as you own the device.
how.s1.p: Snap a picture of your printer. Our AI works out the exact model — no fixed list, we try every printer.
how.s2.p: We detect your printer’s model, generate the matching SMTP settings, and create a dedicated email address for it — plus a walkthrough of exactly where to enter the config on your printer. Can’t identify your model confidently? We show the generic settings screen instead.
how.s3.p: Open your printer’s settings, go to the exact screen we point you to, and enter what we’ve written for you. One time, ever — under five minutes even the first time.
how.s4.p: Press Scan to Email, pick your address, and by the time the scan finishes it’s already in your inbox — automatically archived, always searchable, in under a minute per document.

price.i2: No page limit for ordinary office use. One attachment per e-mail, up to 20 MB; the device will not send a larger one and will say so.
price.i3: On our side the data stays in the EU — the relaying happens on inbox.eu infrastructure in the European Union, in line with the GDPR. Where the scan goes after that is decided by the mailbox you choose.
price.i4: Machines with SMTP authentication and TLS — in practice most office models from Canon, HP, Brother, Epson, Kyocera, Xerox, Ricoh, Konica Minolta, Lexmark and Sharp.

faq.a0: A service that gives your scanner or multifunction printer its own SMTP credentials. The machine already has a “Scan to E-mail” button — what is missing is a mail server that will accept what it sends. Enter the values once, and from then on every scan goes to the address you choose, with no PC in between.
faq.a1: We are building the first version now and expect to launch within the next few months. We will not promise an exact date until we are sure we can hold to it — which is why this page collects sign-ups first. Everyone who signs up gets an e-mail before launch, and the first ten get a year free.
faq.q2: Do I have to buy a new scanner?
faq.a2: Probably not. What you need is a “Scan to E-mail” or SMTP section in the settings, and the machine has to handle SMTP authentication with TLS. Most office models of the last ten years do. Very old machines sometimes handle only outdated encryption — our server will not accept those.
faq.q3: I am on Microsoft 365 — the printer suddenly stopped sending. Will this help?
faq.a3: Yes, this is exactly what it is for. For new Microsoft 365 tenants, SMTP AUTH has been off by default since January 2020. Under Microsoft’s January 2026 timeline nothing changes until December 2026; at the end of December 2026 SMTP AUTH basic auth will be switched off by default for existing tenants too (an administrator will still be able to turn it back on), and Microsoft plans to name the final removal date in the second half of 2027. With ScanInbox the device authenticates with us, not with your 365 tenant, so no Exchange policy, no Azure subscription and no OAuth support on the machine is needed.
faq.q4: Do I need a static IP address or an open port 25?
faq.a4: No. The device connects to our server itself, on port 465 or 587, with a user name and a password. This works behind an ordinary home or office internet connection, including one with a dynamic IP address.
faq.q5: Do I need an IT specialist?
faq.a5: No. You need to be able to open the machine’s settings and copy across the server, the port and the address we have prepared — nothing else. The walkthrough shows what each field is called in your own menu. If it still will not work, reply to our e-mail and we will go through it together.
faq.a6: They travel over an encrypted connection from the device to our server and on to your address; on our side that happens on inbox.eu infrastructure in the European Union, in line with the GDPR. No person reads them, and we do not use the content for anything else. The only thing that happens to the e-mail on the way is an automatic malware and spam check.
faq.q7: Can I receive scans at Gmail or at a work address?
faq.a7: Yes. You can receive at any address — Gmail, Outlook, mail on your own domain. An inbox.eu mailbox is not needed: the sending goes through our SMTP, and that is our side of it.
faq.a8: There is no fixed list — what decides it is whether the machine has an SMTP section with authentication and TLS. In practice that means office models from Canon, HP, Brother, Epson, Kyocera, Xerox, Ricoh, Konica Minolta, Lexmark and Sharp. Tell us your model in the questions after you sign up and we will check it first.
faq.q9: How many devices can I add?
faq.a9: As many as you need. Each one is a separate line in the account, with its own credentials and its own charge. If you have more than ten devices, say so in the sign-up questions — for a fleet that size we look at the price separately.
faq.q10: What do I do if I replace the printer?
faq.a10: Add the new device and get new credentials for it, then switch the old one off. The address the scans arrive at does not change, so nothing has to be carried over by hand.
faq.q11: Does this work at home, not just in the office?
faq.a11: Yes. One printer at home is set up in exactly the same way as ten in an office. After setup, anyone at home types their own address on the device screen and scans to themselves — nothing has to be registered in advance.
faq.a13: Yes. Whoever is scanning types the address on the device screen, so a client, an auditor or a colleague from another department can send a document to themselves without registering anything in advance. Setup is needed once — for the machine itself, not for each person.
faq.q12: What do you do with my e-mail address?
faq.a12: We keep your address, the page language and the answers you give voluntarily after signing up, for one purpose: to tell you about ScanInbox and to understand what to build first. We do not keep your IP address or browser data at all. No other mail, no advertising, and we give it to nobody else. We keep it until launch and for no longer than 24 months. Reply “no” to any e-mail from us and we delete the address and the answers within a few working days.
